pharm: Acts directly on the distal renal tubule (independent of aldosterone) to inhibit sodium reabsorption and reduce potassium and hydrogen excretion, producing a mild natriuresis while conserving potassium; usually combined with hydrochlorothiazide.
quick: Triamterene/HCTZ 37.5/25 mg one or two tablets daily, or 75/50 mg one tablet daily, as a single morning dose
Take with or after food to reduce GI upset; take in the morning to avoid nocturia
Not recommended; diuretics do not prevent toxemia and can reduce placental perfusion
Triamterene appears in breast milk; avoid breastfeeding or the drug
Contraindicated in anuria, acute/chronic renal insufficiency, or significant renal impairment (hyperkalemia)
Use with caution in hepatic disease; can precipitate electrolyte imbalance/encephalopathy
Serum potassium (frequently), renal function, electrolytes, blood glucose, uric acid
summary: Triamterene is a potassium-sparing diuretic that acts on the distal tubule independently of aldosterone, conserving potassium while promoting sodium and water excretion. It is most often given in fixed combination with hydrochlorothiazide to offset thiazide-induced potassium loss in patients with hypertension or edema who cannot risk hypokalemia. Its principal hazard is hyperkalemia, which can be fatal, so serum potassium must be monitored closely, especially in renal impairment, diabetes, and the elderly. It is contraindicated with other potassium-conserving agents, potassium supplements, and significant renal impairment.
indications: Treatment of hypertension or edema in patients who develop hypokalemia on hydrochlorothiazide alone (fixed-combination triamterene/hydrochlorothiazide)
Patients who require a thiazide diuretic and in whom hypokalemia cannot be risked (e.g., on digitalis, history of cardiac arrhythmias)

dosage.d: One or two tablets of triamterene 37.5 mg / hydrochlorothiazide 25 mg once daily as a single dose
dosage.n: Monitor serum potassium; divided dosing increases risk of electrolyte/renal problems

dosage.d: One tablet of triamterene 75 mg / hydrochlorothiazide 50 mg once daily
dosage.n: No experience with more than one 75/50 mg tablet daily

dosage.c: Conversion from HCTZ 50 mg with hypokalemia
dosage.d: Substitute one 75/50 mg combination tablet (or two 37.5/25 mg tablets) daily

admin: Give as a single morning dose to minimize nighttime urination
Take with or after food to reduce gastrointestinal upset
Avoid potassium supplements and potassium-containing salt substitutes
Do not combine with other potassium-sparing agents (spironolactone, amiloride)
Re-check serum potassium and renal function whenever the dose changes or with intercurrent illness
moa: Triamterene acts directly on the distal renal tubule of the nephron, independently of aldosterone, to inhibit the reabsorption of sodium in exchange for potassium and hydrogen ions. By blocking this sodium-potassium exchange it promotes a mild sodium and water diuresis while reducing the renal excretion of potassium (potassium-sparing). When combined with hydrochlorothiazide (which acts in the distal convoluted tubule causing kaliuresis), the two agents have complementary natriuretic effects, and triamterene counteracts the potassium loss caused by the thiazide, helping to maintain normal serum potassium.

absolute: Concurrent use of other potassium-conserving agents (spironolactone, amiloride) or other triamterene-containing products
Potassium supplementation, potassium-containing salt substitutes, or potassium-enriched diets
Anuria, acute and chronic renal insufficiency, or significant renal impairment
Hypersensitivity to triamterene or to sulfonamide-derived thiazide component
relative: Diabetes mellitus (hyperkalemia risk even without renal impairment)
History of renal stones (triamterene calculi reported)

preg: Diuretics are not recommended for routine use in pregnancy and do not prevent toxemia of pregnancy; they may cause fetal/neonatal jaundice, thrombocytopenia, and reduced placental perfusion. Use the combination in pregnancy only when clearly required, recognizing that the hazards may outweigh benefit.
lact: Triamterene appears in breast milk and thiazides are excreted in human milk. Because of the potential for serious adverse effects in the nursing infant, a decision should be made to discontinue nursing or the drug, taking into account its importance to the mother.
renal: Contraindicated in anuria and in acute or chronic renal insufficiency or significant renal impairment because of the high risk of fatal hyperkalemia. Cumulative drug effects and azotemia may occur; the drug can also contribute to triamterene-containing renal calculi. Monitor BUN, creatinine, and potassium closely.
hepatic: Use with caution in patients with hepatic disease; electrolyte and fluid shifts can precipitate hepatic encephalopathy. Severe or progressive hepatic disease is a contraindication. Intrahepatic cholestatic jaundice has been reported.

major: Other potassium-sparing diuretics (spironolactone, amiloride) - severe hyperkalemia; contraindicated
Potassium supplements / potassium-containing salt substitutes - hyperkalemia; contraindicated
ACE inhibitors and angiotensin receptor blockers - markedly increased hyperkalemia risk
Lithium - thiazide reduces lithium clearance, increasing lithium toxicity
moderate: NSAIDs (e.g., indomethacin) - reduced diuretic effect and risk of acute renal failure with triamterene
Antihypertensives - additive blood-pressure lowering; adjust doses
Antidiabetic agents (oral or insulin) - thiazide may raise blood glucose; dosage adjustment may be needed
Corticotropin/corticosteroids - intensified electrolyte (potassium) depletion from thiazide
Skeletal muscle relaxants (e.g., tubocurarine) - thiazide may potentiate
minor: Pressor amines (e.g., norepinephrine) - thiazide may decrease response
interactions.food: Take with food to reduce GI upset; avoid potassium-rich salt substitutes and excessive high-potassium foods.
interactions.alcohol: Alcohol, barbiturates, and narcotics may aggravate orthostatic hypotension.
interactions.diagnostics: May interfere with fluorometric assays (triamterene fluoresces); thiazide can raise serum calcium, glucose, uric acid, and lipids and lower potassium/sodium.

serious: Acute renal failure / acute interstitial nephritis

monitoring: Serum potassium frequently (especially at initiation, dose change, or illness)
Serum electrolytes and renal function (BUN, creatinine)
Blood glucose and serum uric acid
Acid-base status; CBC in long-term use
counsel: Do not take potassium supplements or salt substitutes containing potassium unless told to
Report muscle weakness, fatigue, slow/irregular heartbeat, or numbness/tingling - these can signal high potassium
This medicine may turn your urine bluish - this is harmless
Avoid prolonged sun exposure and use sunscreen (photosensitivity)
Take in the morning, keep all blood-test appointments, and rise slowly to avoid dizziness
pk: Diuresis begins within 2-4 hours of an oral dose
Peak plasma concentration about 1.5-3 hours after dosing
Approximately 1.5-2.5 hours (triamterene); prolonged in renal/hepatic impairment
Store at controlled room temperature (20-25 C); protect from light and moisture
pearls: Hyperkalemia is the key hazard - can be fatal; monitor potassium especially in renal impairment, diabetes, and the elderly
Potassium-sparing: never add KCl supplements, salt substitutes, or another K-sparing agent
Acts on the distal tubule independent of aldosterone (unlike spironolactone)
Most often used as the fixed combination with hydrochlorothiazide to offset thiazide-induced hypokalemia
Can cause harmless blue-green urine fluorescence and rare triamterene renal stones; mild folate antagonist (megaloblastic anemia risk)
missed: If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember unless it is late in the day; do not take it close to bedtime because it can cause nighttime urination. If it is nearly time for your next dose, skip the missed dose and resume your usual schedule. Never double the dose.
overdose: Overdose produces signs of electrolyte imbalance and hyperkalemia (nausea, vomiting, weakness, fatigue, hypotension, and possible cardiac arrhythmias). There is no specific antidote; induce emesis or lavage if recent, and provide supportive care with correction of fluid and electrolyte (especially potassium) imbalance, monitoring renal function and cardiac rhythm. Hemodialysis may be considered for severe hyperkalemia or renal failure.
